analysis.one_liner: Makes foreign oil rigs fully liable when spilled oil reaches U.S. waters, with no damage cap.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in November 2011 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, dying when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 so that if a foreign offshore oil facility spills oil beyond the U.S. exclusive economic zone and that oil reaches, or threatens to reach, U.S. waters, the responsible party must pay the cleanup costs and damages. It removes the current limits on liability for such foreign operators and removes the $1 billion per-incident cap on spending from the government's Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund for these incidents, so more spill money could be drawn if needed. It would close a gap that lets offshore drilling farther out at sea escape the liability rules that apply to domestic drilling.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities whose beaches, fishing grounds, and tourism economies bear the damage when offshore oil from foreign rigs drifts onto U.S. shores, along with taxpayers who would otherwise absorb cleanup costs beyond an operator's liability cap.

how_it_helps.text: Makes each responsible party for a foreign offshore unit liable for removal costs and damages when spilled oil enters, or threatens to enter, U.S. navigable waters or the exclusive economic zone, even if the spill originated beyond the zone.

Eliminates any cap on liability for incidents involving a foreign offshore unit whose oil enters or threatens U.S. waters, so the government and victims could recover the full cost of cleanup and damage.
Removes the $1 billion per-incident limit on expenditures from the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund for these foreign-unit incidents, allowing more federal money to be spent on a large spill response.

analysis.who_pays: Foreign offshore oil operators, which would face unlimited cleanup and damage liability for spills reaching U.S. waters; some of that cost could be passed into the price of oil they produce.

drawbacks.text: Unlimited liability for incidents reaching U.S. waters would raise the cost of operating foreign offshore facilities, and operators may pass some of that cost to consumers through the price of oil.

Lifting the $1 billion per-incident cap on the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund for foreign-unit incidents means the public fund could be drawn on more heavily in a large foreign spill, reducing the resources available for other spills the fund covers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: coastal residents and taxpayers would no longer be left holding cleanup and damage costs from foreign rig spills that reach U.S. waters. The costs fall on the companies causing the risk, and the main downsides — somewhat costlier foreign drilling and heavier possible use of a spill fund that is financed by industry fees — are modest and directly tied to the risk being addressed. The design is narrow and targeted rather than sweeping, so there is little collateral downside for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Menendez introduced the bill on November 9, 2011, with Senator Nelson of Florida joining as an original co-introducer.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the day it was introduced; that is the only action in its history.

Two senators — one Democrat and one Republican — cosponsored the bill, but the committee never held a hearing or vote and the Senate never voted on it before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign offshore oil operators are better off: they remain outside the Oil Pollution Act's framework for spills that start beyond the exclusive economic zone, with the statutory liability caps and the $1 billion trust-fund expenditure limit unchanged, because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought a liability fix for foreign offshore oil spills reaching U.S. waters.

for.name: Sen. Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: Two Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic lead sponsor and a bipartisan pair of cosponsors (one Democrat, one Republican), and no opposition is recorded anywhere in its short history; it was never acted on in committee or on the floor.

industries.industry: Foreign offshore oil and gas operators
industries.note: The bill would make these operators fully liable, with no cap, for cleanup costs and damages when oil from their facilities reaches U.S. waters — including facilities operating beyond the exclusive economic zone whose spills would otherwise largely escape U.S. liability rules. The industry's interest in keeping the liability gap open runs against coastal residents and taxpayers who absorb spill costs.

These industries live on beaches and fisheries that would be contaminated by an uncompensated foreign spill; the bill gives them a liable party to recover damages from instead of leaving the loss with them.
